Image:alt: A giraffe stands tall in a savanna landscape.
Hint 1: My tongue can be almost 50 cm long.
Hint 2: I have a one-of-a-kind spot pattern.
Hint 3: I’m the tallest land animal on Earth.
Fun Facts: A giraffe’s heart can weigh more than 10 kilograms, and it pumps blood all the way up its long neck.
Image Attribution: Photo: Unsplash

Image:alt: A red panda rests on a wooden platform, showing its reddish coat and bushy tail.
Hint 1: I spend most of my day curled up asleep in a tree.
Hint 2: My diet is almost entirely bamboo, even though I'm not closely related to the black-and-white panda.
Hint 3: I have a bushy ringed tail and a reddish coat, and people sometimes call me a 'red cat-bear.'
Fun Facts: Red pandas use their bushy tails as blankets in cold weather and have a false thumb, an extended wrist bone, that helps them grip bamboo stems.
Image Attribution: Photo: Bernard Landgraf, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A pale, gelatinous blobfish with a droopy, saggy face.
Hint 1: I live so deep underwater that the pressure would crush most other fish.
Hint 2: Out of the water, gravity makes me look nothing like I do in my natural habitat.
Hint 3: I've been voted one of the world's ugliest animals, and my saggy face is famous online.
Fun Facts: A blobfish's body is mostly a gel-like substance slightly less dense than water, letting it float just above the sea floor without wasting energy swimming.
Image Attribution: Photo: Alphama, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: scaly anteater, Sunda pangolin, Manis javanica
Image:alt: A scaly pangolin walking across the forest floor.
Hint 1: I'm the only mammal in the world completely covered in scales.
Hint 2: When I feel threatened, I roll up into a tight, armored ball.
Hint 3: I use a long, sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites, much like an anteater.
Fun Facts: A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its own body, and it retracts into a pouch near its pelvis when not in use.
Image Attribution: Photo: Ari hidayat99, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: unicorn of the sea, Monodon monoceros
Image:alt: An old illustration of a narwhal showing its long, spiraled tusk.
Hint 1: I live year-round in cold Arctic waters.
Hint 2: Males of my species usually grow a single long, spiraled tusk.
Hint 3: That tusk is actually an overgrown tooth, and it's inspired centuries of unicorn legends.
Fun Facts: A narwhal's tusk is a canine tooth that can grow up to 3 meters long and is packed with nerve endings, possibly helping it sense changes in the water.
Image Attribution: Photo: The Public Domain Review, Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A platypus being held near a riverbank, showing its duck-like bill.
Hint 1: I lay eggs, even though I'm a mammal.
Hint 2: I have a soft, sensitive bill that I use to detect prey underwater.
Hint 3: I look like a mix of a duck, a beaver, and an otter, and the males among us have a venomous spur on their hind legs.
Fun Facts: When platypuses were first described to European scientists, many believed the pelt was an elaborate hoax stitched together from other animals.
Image Attribution: Photo: TwoWings, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A pale pink axolotl with feathery external gills, resting underwater.
Hint 1: I never really grow up, I keep my juvenile features my whole life.
Hint 2: If I lose a limb, or even part of my heart or brain, I can regrow it.
Hint 3: I'm a salamander with feathery external gills and a face that always looks like it's smiling.
Fun Facts: Axolotls are critically endangered in the wild in Mexico, even though they're one of the most common amphibians kept in captivity worldwide.
Image Attribution: Photo: Marius Maehlen (Mariblubb), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A chameleon gripping a branch with its curled tail and independently rotating eyes.
Hint 1: Each of my eyes can swivel and focus independently of the other.
Hint 2: I'm famous for changing color, though it's more about mood and temperature than blending in.
Hint 3: I have a long, sticky tongue I can shoot out faster than a blink to catch insects.
Fun Facts: A chameleon's tongue can extend to more than one and a half times its own body length and accelerates faster than a fighter jet.
Image Attribution: Photo: Zeynel Cebeci, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Aliases: three-toed sloth, brown-throated sloth, Bradypus variegatus
Image:alt: A sloth hanging from a tree branch, moving slowly through the canopy.
Hint 1: I move so slowly that algae grows in my fur.
Hint 2: I spend almost my entire life hanging upside down in trees.
Hint 3: I'm famous as one of the slowest-moving mammals on Earth.
Fun Facts: Sloths only leave their trees to go to the bathroom about once a week, and the trip can be dangerous since it's when they're most vulnerable to predators.
Image Attribution: Photo: Krunal Desai, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A seahorse floating upright in the water, its tail curled around a strand of seagrass.
Hint 1: In my species, it's the males who carry the babies, not the females.
Hint 2: I swim upright, and I'm a famously weak swimmer despite living in the open ocean.
Hint 3: My head looks like a horse's, which is exactly how I got my name.
Fun Facts: Male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a specialized pouch and give birth to fully-formed babies, one of the only examples of male pregnancy in the animal kingdom.
Image Attribution: Photo: FASTILY, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: An octopus crawling across the seafloor, its arms spread across the rocks.
Hint 1: I have three hearts and blue blood.
Hint 2: I can squeeze my entire boneless body through any gap bigger than my beak.
Hint 3: I have eight arms lined with suckers, and I'm famous for being one of the smartest invertebrates alive.
Fun Facts: An octopus can change both the color and texture of its skin in less than a second to blend almost perfectly into its surroundings.
Image Attribution: Photo: Martijn Klijnstra, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A bright pink flamingo standing on one leg in shallow water.
Hint 1: The pink or reddish color of my feathers actually comes from what I eat.
Hint 2: I usually stand and sleep balanced on just one leg.
Hint 3: I'm known for my long legs, curved neck, and bright pink feathers, and I usually live in large flocks.
Fun Facts: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat, and in captivity they can turn pale without the right diet.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A close-up of a monarch butterfly's orange and black wings.
Hint 1: I make one of the longest migrations of any insect on Earth.
Hint 2: My caterpillar stage eats almost nothing but milkweed, which makes me toxic to most predators.
Hint 3: I'm an orange-and-black butterfly, and no single one of us completes the whole migration round trip, it takes multiple generations.
Fun Facts: Monarch butterflies that migrate south in the fall can live up to 8 months, far longer than the few weeks a typical summer generation survives.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles Patrick Ewing, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A koala climbing a eucalyptus tree trunk.
Hint 1: I sleep around 20 hours a day.
Hint 2: My diet is almost entirely eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals.
Hint 3: I'm a tree-dwelling marsupial from Australia, often mistaken for a bear, even though I'm not one.
Fun Facts: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human fingerprints that they can be difficult to tell apart even under a microscope.
Image Attribution: Photo: Diliff (David Iliff), CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A hedgehog walking through grass, covered in short spines.
Hint 1: When I feel threatened, I roll into a tight ball covered in spines.
Hint 2: I'm mostly active at night and spend the day sleeping in a nest of leaves.
Hint 3: I'm covered in thousands of short spines instead of fur on my back.
Fun Facts: A hedgehog can have around 5,000 to 7,000 spines, and each one is a modified hair made of keratin, the same protein in human fingernails.
Image Attribution: Photo: Hrald, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: An aardvark with a long snout and large ears, standing on all fours.
Hint 1: I dig burrows and come out mostly at night to feed.
Hint 2: My name comes from an Afrikaans word meaning 'earth pig,' even though I'm not related to pigs.
Hint 3: I use powerful claws and a long snout to break into termite mounds and eat with a sticky tongue.
Fun Facts: Aardvarks can seal their nostrils shut to keep dust and insects out while digging or eating termites.
Image Attribution: Photo: Theo Kruse (Burgers' Zoo), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: An orange and white striped clownfish swimming among the tentacles of a sea anemone.
Hint 1: I live in a close partnership with a sea creature whose sting would hurt most other fish.
Hint 2: I'm immune to the stinging tentacles of the anemone I call home.
Hint 3: I'm orange with white stripes, and I was made famous by an animated movie about a lost fish.
Fun Facts: Clownfish are all born male, and the largest, most dominant fish in a group changes into a female when needed.
Image Attribution: Photo: Triniti14045, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A fully inflated, spiky pufferfish floating in open water.
Hint 1: I can swallow huge amounts of water to make myself much bigger when threatened.
Hint 2: Many of my relatives contain a toxin many times more poisonous than cyanide.
Hint 3: When fully inflated, I look like a round, spiky ball floating in the water.
Fun Facts: A pufferfish's stomach can stretch to many times its normal size in seconds, letting it balloon into a spiky sphere almost too big for predators to swallow.
Image Attribution: Photo: Adedotun Ajibade (Dotun55), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A peacock in side profile, showing its long, iridescent tail feathers.
Hint 1: Only the males of my species grow the famous, dramatic tail.
Hint 2: I fan out my long tail feathers covered in eye-like patterns to attract a mate.
Hint 3: I'm a large, colorful bird best known for my iridescent blue-green tail feathers.
Fun Facts: A peacock's train feathers aren't its tail at all, they're long upper tail-covert feathers, and it can have over 200 of them.
Image Attribution: Photo: Anup Hela, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A toco toucan perched on a branch, showing its huge orange beak.
Hint 1: My oversized beak is actually much lighter than it looks.
Hint 2: I use my huge, colorful beak to reach fruit at the end of thin branches.
Hint 3: I'm famous for my enormous orange beak, which can be nearly a third of my total body length.
Fun Facts: A toucan's huge beak helps regulate its body temperature, acting almost like a built-in radiator to release excess heat.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A spotted leopard gecko resting on sandy ground.
Hint 1: Unlike most geckos, I have movable eyelids and can blink.
Hint 2: If a predator grabs my tail, I can drop it and grow a new one.
Hint 3: I'm a small, spotted lizard that's one of the most popular pet reptiles in the world.
Fun Facts: Leopard geckos store extra fat in their tails, so a plump tail is usually a sign of a healthy, well-fed gecko.
Image Attribution: Photo: Brandon Downey, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A close-up of a green iguana's head, showing its spines and dewlap.
Hint 1: I have a row of spines running down my back and a flap of skin under my chin.
Hint 2: I'm mostly herbivorous and spend much of my time basking in trees near water.
Hint 3: I'm a large, often green lizard, and I can drop into water and swim away if threatened.
Fun Facts: Iguanas have a light-sensing 'third eye' on top of their heads that can detect changes in light and shadow, helping them spot predators from above.
Image Attribution: Photo: Ianaré Sévi, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A red ladybug with black spots resting on a green leaf.
Hint 1: Despite my name, I can be male or female.
Hint 2: My bright, spotted colors warn predators that I taste bad.
Hint 3: I'm a small, round beetle usually red or orange with black spots, and gardeners love me because I eat aphids.
Fun Facts: When threatened, ladybugs can release a foul-smelling yellow fluid from their leg joints, a defense called reflex bleeding.
Image Attribution: Photo: Nursa Sherli Yoanita, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A dragonfly perched on a twig, its transparent wings spread out.
Hint 1: I can fly in every direction, including straight backward and hovering in place.
Hint 2: Before I grew wings, I lived underwater as a fierce nymph for months or even years.
Hint 3: I'm an insect with two pairs of long, transparent wings and a slender, often colorful body.
Fun Facts: Dragonflies have nearly 360-degree vision thanks to eyes made up of up to 30,000 individual lenses each.
Image Attribution: Photo: Christophe95, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: Two sea otters floating on their backs at the water's surface.
Hint 1: I often float on my back at the water's surface, sometimes holding hands with others of my kind so we don't drift apart while sleeping.
Hint 2: I use tools, like rocks, to crack open shellfish while floating.
Hint 3: I'm a marine mammal known for my thick, dense fur, the densest fur of any animal.
Fun Facts: Sea otters have up to a million hairs per square inch of skin, the densest fur in the animal kingdom, which traps air to keep them warm since they lack blubber.
Image Attribution: Photo: Joe Robertson, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A tiny tarsier clinging to a branch, its enormous eyes wide open at night.
Hint 1: Each of my eyeballs is bigger than my entire brain.
Hint 2: I can rotate my head almost 180 degrees in each direction to spot prey at night.
Hint 3: I'm a tiny nocturnal primate with enormous eyes and long fingers, found in Southeast Asian forests.
Fun Facts: A tarsier's eyes are so large and fixed in their sockets that it can't roll them at all, its extreme head rotation makes up for it.
Image Attribution: Photo: Seshadri.K.S, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A capybara resting calmly near the water's edge.
Hint 1: I'm the largest rodent in the world.
Hint 2: I'm extremely social and often seen lounging in groups near water.
Hint 3: I'm a large, calm, semi-aquatic rodent from South America, often shown relaxing with other animals riding on my back.
Fun Facts: Capybaras are so comfortable in water that they can sleep while floating, and they're known to happily share space with birds, monkeys, and even caimans.
Image Attribution: Photo: Karoly Lorentey, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: An emperor penguin standing on Antarctic ice.
Hint 1: The males of my species incubate a single egg on their feet through the harshest part of the Antarctic winter.
Hint 2: I'm the largest of all penguin species.
Hint 3: I'm a flightless, black-and-white seabird that huddles together with thousands of others to survive extreme cold.
Fun Facts: Male emperor penguins fast for around two months while incubating their egg, surviving entirely on stored fat reserves.
Image Attribution: Photo: Samuel Blanc, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A puffin standing on a rocky cliff, showing its brightly colored beak.
Hint 1: I can carry a dozen or more small fish crosswise in my beak at once.
Hint 2: I spend most of the year out at sea and only come to land to breed in burrows.
Hint 3: I'm a small seabird with a brightly colored, triangular beak, often called the 'clown of the sea.'
Fun Facts: A puffin's colorful beak actually fades in winter and grows a brighter outer layer again each breeding season.
Image Attribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A soft gray chinchilla sitting upright.
Hint 1: I take dust baths instead of water baths to keep my fur clean.
Hint 2: My fur is so dense that up to 60 hairs can grow from a single hair follicle.
Hint 3: I'm a small, soft, gray rodent from the Andes mountains, and I have one of the densest furs of any land mammal.
Fun Facts: A chinchilla's fur is so tightly packed that fleas can't survive in it, since there's no room for them to move around.
Image Attribution: Photo: Jaime E. Jimenez, CC BY, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A small fennec fox with large ears peeking out from behind a rock.
Hint 1: I have the largest ears relative to my body size of any fox.
Hint 2: My oversized ears help me radiate heat and hear prey moving underground in the desert.
Hint 3: I'm the smallest fox species in the world, with pale fur and huge ears, native to the Sahara.
Fun Facts: A fennec fox's kidneys are so efficient that it can survive for long periods without ever drinking water, getting most of its moisture from food.
Image Attribution: Photo: Anass ERRIHANI, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A hawksbill sea turtle swimming over a coral reef.
Hint 1: My narrow, pointed beak helps me reach into crevices on coral reefs to feed.
Hint 2: My shell has an overlapping, almost tile-like pattern of scutes.
Hint 3: I'm a critically endangered sea turtle named for my beak-like mouth, and I mostly eat sponges.
Fun Facts: Hawksbill sea turtles can eat sponges that are toxic to most other animals, and they help keep coral reefs healthy by controlling sponge growth.
Image Attribution: Photo: DRVIP93, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A translucent jellyfish drifting with its tentacles trailing behind.
Hint 1: I have no brain, no heart, and no bones, yet my kind has existed for more than 500 million years.
Hint 2: I'm made up of about 95 percent water.
Hint 3: I drift through the ocean with a soft, bell-shaped body and trailing tentacles that can sting.
Fun Facts: Some jellyfish species are considered biologically immortal, able to reverse their aging process and revert to an earlier stage of life under stress.
Image Attribution: Photo: JustPere, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

Image:alt: A star-nosed mole showing the ring of fleshy tentacles around its nose.
Hint 1: I can identify and eat prey faster than the human eye can follow, in under a quarter of a second.
Hint 2: I spend most of my life underground or in water, and I'm nearly blind.
Hint 3: I have 22 fleshy, finger-like tentacles ringing my nose that I use to feel my way around and find food.
Fun Facts: A star-nosed mole's nose has more touch receptors than a human hand, packed into an organ small enough to fit on a fingertip.
Image Attribution: Photo: US National Park Service, Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons
